text: I’ll model the fluid region directly as a planar channel and later extrude it by a small, single-cell thickness for OpenFOAM. Because only the main width and approximate total length were specified, the first coarse design assumes four alternating bypasses, each spanning 24 mm axially, extending 15 mm from the main-channel centreline, with the same 6 mm passage width. I’ll first construct and inspect that fluid footprint at low geometric resolution.

The coarse footprint is a single connected face with four open bypass paths and no enclosed holes, so it is suitable for a conformal quasi-2D mesh. Next I’ll extract its ordered outer boundary and verify that the only two 6 mm terminal edges are the intended inlet and outlet before creating the extruded mesh.
The Boolean result is a build123d `Sketch` container rather than a bare `Face`; I’ll take its sole face explicitly and repeat the boundary check.

The inlet and outlet are now tied to explicit CAD edges (0 and 52), each measured at exactly 6 mm. I’ll discretize the remaining curved CAD boundary to about 0.8 mm chord length, preserving those edge labels, and verify closure and area before meshing.

The 19.8% area mismatch shows that `Wire.edges()` did not return traversal order even though the wire is closed; using it directly would create crossed boundary segments. I’ll query the installed build123d wire-ordering API before rebuilding the polygon.
The installed API provides `Wire.order_edges()`. I’ll use that traversal and identify the two already-validated terminal CAD edges by their exact endpoint coordinates and 6 mm length.

The wire traversal is now correct; the remaining area difference is intentional topology that the first check omitted: each bypass encloses a solid teardrop island, so the fluid face has inner wires as well as its outer wire. I’ll enumerate and discretize all wires, then verify that outer area minus hole areas matches the CAD face.

All five loops close, and the polygonal net area agrees with CAD to 0.012%. I’ll now extrude the footprint by an assumed 1 mm with one cell through thickness, create a roughly 1 mm in-plane triangular mesh (extruded to prisms), and assign inlet/outlet from their preserved CAD-edge labels; all other side surfaces become `walls`, while the two planes become `frontAndBack`.
The Gmsh construction itself reached extrusion, but a local typo referenced Python’s built-in `next` instead of the returned `ext` list. I’ll rerun that mesh-export step with the corrected variable.

The coarse Gmsh run produced 24,210 tetrahedra. Although valid 3D cells, tetrahedra are unsuitable for an OpenFOAM `empty` front/back pair because they do not form a strict single prismatic layer. I’ll regenerate the same footprint with recombined extrusion, which should produce one layer of triangular prisms.

The corrected mesh contains 8,070 six-node prisms in exactly one extruded layer. I’ll convert it to OpenFOAM, set only `frontAndBack` to `empty`, and inspect the resulting patch table before running quality checks.

Conversion preserved all 8,070 prisms and the four intended patches; `frontAndBack` contains the paired planar faces, while inlet and outlet each contain eight side faces. I’ll now render the converted OpenFOAM mesh from above so the cell distribution and all four bypass islands can be checked visually.

The top view confirms a connected straight passage with four alternating teardrop bypasses and no unintended cross-connections. The footprint is naturally slender, but the roughly six cells across every 6 mm passage are visible. I’ll now run OpenFOAM’s full topology and geometry checks.

`checkMesh` did not reach the mesh because this OpenFOAM build requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for extended checks. I’ll add minimal non-solving dictionaries and rerun the same check.

The extended check found seven under-determined cells and 13 low-weight faces, traced to 10.6 µm sliver segments left by CAD Boolean intersections—far below the 1 mm coarse mesh scale. I’ll defeature only boundary segments shorter than 0.20 mm, while preserving the inlet/outlet labels, and quantify the resulting dimensional and area change before remeshing.

Removing 16 sliver segments raises the minimum boundary edge to 0.272 mm while changing fluid area by only −0.0114%; both terminals retain all eight subdivisions. I’ll regenerate the one-layer prism mesh from this cleaned boundary.
The cleaned coarse mesh contains 7,518 prisms. I’ll replace the previous OpenFOAM mesh with this version and restore the explicit `empty` type on `frontAndBack`.
The replacement mesh has the intended 7,518-prism single layer and patch counts. I’ll rerun the full topology and geometry checks to confirm that cleaning removed the quality failures.

The cleaned mesh now passes all extended OpenFOAM checks: maximum non-orthogonality 23.30°, maximum skewness 0.435, minimum determinant 0.0521, and one connected region. I’ll export the four named mesh patches as separate STL surfaces for downstream inspection and advisory closure checks.

`foamToSurface` only offers a combined export. To preserve patch names, I’ll instead read the checked OpenFOAM boundary faces directly—whose winding is already outward from the fluid—and triangulate each patch into its own STL.

The four STL exports contain the complete checked boundary with outward OpenFOAM face winding. I’ll make one final top-view image of the cleaned mesh, selecting only the internal cell block so the displayed cell count is not inflated by boundary faces.

The reader nests its blocks differently than expected, so the diagnostic tried to query a cell count on another `MultiBlock`. I’ll traverse the block tree recursively and select the dataset explicitly named `internalMesh`.

The final checked view confirms the intended four-loop topology and the cleaned 7,518-cell mesh. All requested dimensions were measured; the unspecified loop proportions and quasi-2D depth are documented as assumptions.
